docs.title: MarathonTS
docs.text:
A benchmark of long synthetic time series from window assembly and long-series generators.

Many uses of synthetic time series need a series much longer than the windows a generative model is trained on. MarathonTS compares the two ways to obtain one under a single protocol: assembly from a pool of short generated windows (which windows, in what order, how the seams are processed) and long-series generators (Diffusion-TS, Chronos, TimesFM, Timestral). Every method yields a series of the same length; the benchmark measures its fidelity to the real data, its utility for models trained on it, its memorisation of the training data and its cost. The statistics (rankings, research questions with tests and uncertainty, a pre-specified confirmatory family) are a separate stage that reads the benchmark tables.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
A smoke test runs the whole pipeline on 2 datasets (ett, bike), 2 seeds and small models (Config.quick()); both datasets are downloaded without credentials. Local run in one environment (Linux or macOS, Python 3.11 or 3.12, git on the path):

git clone https://github.com/zypl-ai/MarathonTS.git
cd MarathonTS
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
git clone https://github.com/Y-debug-sys/Diffusion-TS.git external/Diffusion-TS
git -C external/Diffusion-TS checkout 566307e6cf2d8095e58de4c6e3a6ae965b69b5b5

python -m marathonts.bench.run all --quick                            # data → pools → series → fidelity → utility → tables
python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run --artifacts-dir artifacts/quick   # reports → artifacts/quick/reports/

The benchmark is also installable as a package, pip install marathonts (the same commands; see Guide C, C0). The pretrained generators (Chronos, TimesFM, Timestral) download their weights from Hugging Face on first use. The same test with Docker: Guide A, A2; in Colab: Guide B, B4.

docs.title: Results and how to read them
docs.text:
Stage 7 (python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run) writes four Markdown reports to artifacts/<profile>/reports/:

Report Contents OVERALL.md the overall leaderboard: fidelity on the core metrics and utility with equal weights, noise-aware ranks, robustness checks LEADERBOARD.md the ranking of every method in every slice: the four rankings, core-metric rankings, privacy, cost METRIC_VALUES.md values of the core fidelity metrics and the primary utility metrics by reference, dataset, task, model and split REPORT.md research questions RQ0–RQ9, the confirmatory family C1–C4, the case study CS1–CS15

Their Parquet tables are in artifacts/<profile>/overall/, leaderboard/, metric_values/ and hypotheses/; the benchmark tables they are computed from are in artifacts/<profile>/tables/. artifacts/run_h200/ holds the tables and reports of the main run and artifacts/run_l4/ those of the replication run; your own runs are written to artifacts/<profile>/. The full artifacts of both runs (pools, series, fidelity and utility records, labels) are on Hugging Face, and the rankings of both runs can be explored in the interactive leaderboard, which opens on the main run. The metrics are defined in METRICS.md, the statistical procedure and the reading of the verdicts in HYPOTHESES.md.

docs.title: Published runs and the main leaderboard
docs.text:

docs.title: Change the configuration
docs.text: Every setting is a field of Config (marathonts/bench/config.py); three profiles (min, mid, max) are ready-made sets of values. docs.title: Proprietary methods
docs.text:
Three components are proprietary methods of zypl.ai under development: the assembler zseries (vae_zseries and its seam-processing variants) and, in the main run of the paper, two generators of the zEDGE family:

  • zEDGE — a pool generator: it generates the window pool that the assemblers turn into a long series (pool prefix zedge, methods zedge_zseries, zedge_greedy, …);
  • zEDGE_TS — a long-series generator: it generates the long series directly, without a pool. One sequence model over the latent vectors of zEDGE is trained per dataset and shared by the seeds; it is sampled in two modes:
  • zedge_ts_long — block inpainting: the latent sequence is built in blocks of 12 latent vectors, each next block conditioned on the last three latent vectors of the previous one;
  • zedge_ts_ar — autoregressive: one latent vector at a time, conditioned on the preceding 11; slower, but every step agrees with a longer context.

In both modes every latent vector is decoded into a window, and neighbouring windows (overlap T/2) are joined by a cosine crossfade.

They are evaluated as black boxes under the same protocol as every other method: their results are published in the tables (Config.frozen_methods) and enter the rankings and the analysis, their code is not part of the repository, and their results cannot be reproduced from it. No open method uses any of their components. Every ranking can be recomputed with any set of methods excluded (--rank-exclude). The paper states the competing interests of the authors.

docs.title: Methods compared
docs.text:
Ways to assemble a long series from a pool of N generated windows (which K windows, in what order, how the seams are processed) and long-series generators. vae_zseries is zseries, the proprietary assembler of zypl.ai (under development), on the same pool: its results are published (Config.frozen_methods), its code is not part of the repository. Its results and those of its seam-processing variants vae_zseries_{xfade,wsola,quilt} enter the tables and the analysis as published; the pipeline does not run them.

Only methods whose series enter the benchmark tables are listed here: each outputs a series of length K·T in the same channels and enters the utility test of BENCHMARK.md (Protocol: utility) like any other series. Methods that were considered but not included are in LITERATURE.md.

In the benchmark (BENCHMARK.md) all profiles use all methods of sections A and B except CSDI, plus Diffusion-TS, Chronos, TimesFM and Timestral from section C; the noise twin vae_rand_b runs in mid and max only. All methods of A and B take the same VAE pool (min: 300 windows); the methods of B are applied on top of the vae_zseries path (published results; max: in addition on top of every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting, run by the pipeline).

Each alternative assembler uses the seam criterion of its own literature, nothing taken from vae_zseries. The three solvers (greedy, ATSP, PCTSP) are general-purpose optimisers without a seam criterion of their own; they get the jump at the seam — the Euclidean distance between the last point of a window and the first point of the next, over every channel (value and hour of week, all on [0, 1]) — the frame distance of video textures (Schödl et al. 2000).

"In-house" in the "Code" column means that there is no ready-made library, but the method takes 10–40 lines on top of the pool (marathonts/bench/assemblers.py).

docs.title: B. Seam processing
docs.text:
Applied on top of the vae_zseries path (min, mid: the published results vae_zseries_{xfade,wsola,quilt}; max: in addition on top of every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting, which has its own boundary cut). Because of the overlap the series is shorter than K·T, so additional windows are taken to reach the required length.

Method Idea Year Paper Code Overlap-add / crossfade Windows overlap by o points and are blended with window weights (Hann) 1977 Allen J., Rabiner L. A unified approach to short-time Fourier analysis and synthesis. Proc. IEEE 65(11), 1977 in-house + scipy.signal.windows.hann WSOLA Before blending, the next window is shifted within a tolerance to maximise the correlation in the overlap 1993 Verhelst W., Roelands M. docs.title: Benchmark: pipeline
docs.text: The benchmark (marathonts/bench/) generates long synthetic series with every method on every dataset and measures their fidelity, utility and cost. Statistics and conclusions are separate, in the hypothesis testing (HYPOTHESES.md, section 7), which reads the benchmark tables. Everything is stored in Parquet; each part (dataset, generator, assembler, model, metric, target) is plugged in through a registry — EXTENDING.md.

docs.text:

Profiles write to their own folders — data/processed/<profile>/ and artifacts/<profile>/ — so results do not mix; mid uses the prepared data of min (they are identical). Below, artifacts/… is short for artifacts/<profile>/….

When a generator model is shared by several seeds, the seed still changes pool sampling and random paths, and the training time of the shared model is recorded for every seed (used in RQ6). The weights of the shared model are artifacts/<profile>/generators/<ds>/<generator>/replica<k>.parquet. Any setting can be changed on its own (Config.profile("min", hpo=True)). Target parameters (exogenous, see below): marathonts/bench/target_params.json for min and mid (same data) and marathonts/bench/target_params_max.json for max — thresholds are computed on the train of their own split, because the train of profile min falls into the val and OOT of profile max.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Generators with conflicting dependencies run in their own environments. Environments communicate only through Parquet artifacts: the pools stage trains the pool generator in its environment and writes the pool to artifacts/pools/, while generate and everything after it run in the main environment and read the pool from there. TensorFlow is never imported in the main environment.

docs.text: Docker, Colab notebooks or local environments, each with a smoke test, the full run and re-running only the analysis — GETTING_STARTED.md. Settings and their effect on the stages — CONFIGURATION.md.

docs.title: What is compared
docs.text:
Method How the series of length K·T is obtained vae_zseries pool of N VAE windows (min: 300) → zseries, the proprietary assembler of zypl.ai (under development); its results are published (Config.frozen_methods), its code is not part of the repository (the case-study method) vae_rand the same pool, K random windows in random order vae_rand_b the same with another permutation seed (noise estimate; mid and max only) vae_greedy the same pool: greedy nearest neighbour by the jump at the seam from a random window vae_atsp asymmetric travelling salesman problem over the whole pool by the jump at the seam (LKH, elkai); the cheapest segment of K windows is taken from the tour vae_pctsp prize-collecting TSP (OR-Tools): choice of K windows out of N and their order at once by the jump at the seam, search up to pctsp_solutions = 2000 solutions (reproducible), at most pctsp_time_s = 60 s per unit vae_mbb matched-block bootstrap (Carlstein et al. 1998): Markov chain over the pool, P(i→j) ∝ exp(−½ (jump_ij / h)²), h = mbb_bandwidth (1) × median jump vae_knn k-nearest-neighbour resampling (Lall & Sharma 1996): the next window among the k = √N whose first point is nearest to the last point of the current one, weight ∝ 1/rank vae_quilting image quilting (Efros & Freeman 2001): the next window at random among those whose overlap error (12 points) is within 1.1 × the best, the overlap cut at the minimum-error point vae_herding kernel herding: K windows by MMD to the train windows, random order vae_zseries_xfade (published results, as vae_zseries_wsola and vae_zseries_quilt) the vae_zseries path, windows overlap by join_overlap = 12 points and are blended with a Hann window vae_zseries_wsola the same, but the next window is first shifted by up to 12 points towards the best correlation in the overlap (WSOLA) vae_zseries_quilt in the overlap the series switches to the next window at the point of smallest difference (the boundary cut of image quilting in 1D) diffusion_ts Diffusion-TS is trained on the same windows; the first window is generated, each next one is extended by imputation from the tail of the previous one (context T/2); the calendar is given, only the value is generated chronos Chronos samples a trajectory of K·T continuing the last 512 points of train, in chunks of 64 timesfm TimesFM 3.0, zero-shot: the median forecast of the K·T steps after train, the whole train as context (up to 15 360 points) timestral Timestral 209M (Mistral), zero-shot: the median forecast of the K·T steps after train, the whole train as context (up to 32 768 points), block by block

A method is "pool generator + assembler (+ seam processing)" or a "long-series generator" (marathonts/bench/methods.py). Built-in components: pool generators tsgm_vae, sdv_par (SDV PARSynthesizer), real_windows; assemblers random, random_b, greedy, atsp, pctsp, mbb, knn, quilt_sel, herding (marathonts/bench/assemblers.py; the zseries assembler is registered by name only, without code); seam processing crossfade, wsola, quilt (marathonts/bench/joiners.py: the overlap shortens the series, so the assembler returns more than K windows — 33–35 in min — and the series is cut to K·T); long-series generators diffusion_ts, chronos, timesfm, timestral. Custom ones go through the registry. The set of assemblers is defined once (STITCH_SUITE) and run on each pool generator from Config.pool_suites (default {"vae": "tsgm_vae"}; another generator is one more entry, methods <prefix>_zseries, <prefix>_rand, …, EXTENDING.md). Custom assemblers, seam processing and long-series generators are plugged in with a plugin and one line of config (plugins, extra_assemblers, extra_joiners, long_methods, EXTENDING.md) and automatically join the set on every pool. All assemblers of one set take the same pool, so vae_* differ only in the choice, order and joining of windows. The alternative assemblers use the seam criteria of their own literature (BASELINES.md); the solvers (greedy, ATSP, PCTSP) get the jump at the seam — the Euclidean distance between the last point of a window and the first point of the next over every channel. Seam processing runs over the assemblers of smooth_paths (min, mid: the vae_zseries path, published results; any list can be set, e.g. ["greedy", "atsp"]); with smooth_paths="all" (max) every seam processing runs over every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting (it has its own cut) — vae_greedy_xfade, vae_atsp_quilt, … The random path has a single variant, vae_rand, plus the noise twin vae_rand_b in mid and max. The rankings leave out the seam-processing variants unless every assembler has them (rank_exclude, HYPOTHESES.md §3, RQ1); vae_quilting is one method (choice and cut), not a variant, and is ranked. Any method or component is switched off by name (disabled). Results published without their code are listed in frozen_methods (default: vae_zseries, vae_zseries_xfade, vae_zseries_wsola, vae_zseries_quilt): no stage runs them, collect carries their rows into the tables where the run has the settings of their results (tables/frozen.json), and the analysis ranks them like any other method (CONFIGURATION.md, "Switching methods on and off").

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: The common ground of every method: the same channels and windows, the same pool generator for the assembly methods, the same utility test. The code lives in bench/ (data.py, generators/builtin.py, tasks.py, utility.py); the snippets below show the logic.

docs.title: Data: channels and windows
docs.text:
The generator and the assembler work with windows (n, T, 3) in [0, 1]:

  • channel 0 — series value, min-max on train;
  • channels 1–2 — calendar: (sin + 1) / 2, (cos + 1) / 2 of the hour of week.
import numpy as np
from numpy.lib.stride_tricks import sliding_window_view

HOURS_PER_WEEK = 168

def to_channels(values, how, lo, hi):
    a = 2 * np.pi * how / HOURS_PER_WEEK
    return np.column_stack([(values - lo) / (hi - lo),
                            (np.sin(a) + 1) / 2, (np.cos(a) + 1) / 2]).astype(np.float32)

def from_channels(X, lo, hi):
    """Back: values and hour of week (the synthetic calendar is the one the generator produced)."""
    values = X[:, 0] * (hi - lo) + lo
    a = np.arctan2(2 * X[:, 1] - 1, 2 * X[:, 2] - 1)
    how = np.mod(np.rint(a / (2 * np.pi) * HOURS_PER_WEEK), HOURS_PER_WEEK).astype(int)
    return values, how

def slide(X, T, s):
    """Windows of length T with stride s; windows with NaN are dropped."""
    W = sliding_window_view(X, (T, X.shape[1]))[::s, 0]
    return np.ascontiguousarray(W[~np.isnan(W).any(axis=(1, 2))], dtype=np.float32)

# train = values[:n_train], how = hour of week of each row
lo, hi = np.nanmin(train), np.nanmax(train)
X_train = to_channels(train, how[:n_train], lo, hi)        # (n_train, 3)

Window parameters (computed on train only; marathonts/bench/data.py, window_layout):

Parameter Rule min T window length, one week of hours, the same for every dataset (Config.T) 168 s slicing stride: max(1, (n_train − T) // max_windows), max_windows = 5000 1 K number of windows in the assembly: round(n_train / T), as much synthetic data as train 30 N pool size: max(pool_size, pool_mult · K) = max(300, 2K); the assembler takes windows without replacement, so N ≥ K is required 300

The last 10% of train (holdout_frac) is cut off as holdout for early stopping of the generators; between it and the rest of train (core) there is an embargo of embargo = 168 rows. Core and holdout windows do not overlap.

X_core = slide(X_train[:core_end], T, s)
X_hold = slide(X_train[hold_start:], T, s)

docs.title: Pool generator: VAE
docs.text:
Recipe: tsgm vae_conv5 + BetaVAE, latent 16, β = 2, Adam 1e-3, batch 64, up to 400 epochs. Early stopping on holdout loss (z = z_mean), patience 50 epochs, the best weights are kept. The first 150 epochs (vae_min_epochs) do not stop and are not considered for the best weights: holdout minima at epochs 4–23 give an almost flat pool (beijing_pm25, pjm, ett). Sampling: z ~ N(0, 1) · 0.5, the output is clipped to [0, 1].

import os; os.environ.setdefault("KERAS_BACKEND", "tensorflow")
import keras, tensorflow as tf, tsgm

LATENT, BETA, EPOCHS, PATIENCE, MIN_EPOCHS, NOISE = 16, 2.0, 400, 50, 150, 0.5

arch = tsgm.models.zoo["vae_conv5"](seq_len=T, feat_dim=3, latent_dim=LATENT)
vae = tsgm.models.cvae.BetaVAE(arch.encoder, arch.decoder, beta=BETA)
vae.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3))

def holdout_loss(X):
    zm, zlv, _ = vae.encoder(X, training=False)
    rec = vae.decoder(zm, training=False)
    r = tf.reduce_mean(vae._get_reconstruction_loss(X, rec))
    kl = tf.reduce_mean(tf.reduce_sum(-0.5 * (1 + zlv - zm ** 2 - tf.exp(zlv)), axis=1))
    return float(r + kl)

best, best_ep, best_w = np.inf, -1, None
for ep in range(EPOCHS):
    vae.fit(X_core, epochs=1, batch_size=64, verbose=0)
    hl = holdout_loss(X_hold)
    if ep + 1 < MIN_EPOCHS:
        continue
    if hl < best:
        best, best_ep = hl, ep
        best_w = vae.encoder.get_weights() + vae.decoder.get_weights()
    if ep - best_ep >= PATIENCE:
        break
ne = len(vae.encoder.get_weights())
vae.encoder.set_weights(best_w[:ne]); vae.decoder.set_weights(best_w[ne:])

# pool: N windows (N, T, 3)
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
z = (rng.standard_normal((N, LATENT)) * NOISE).astype(np.float32)
pool = np.clip(np.nan_to_num(np.asarray(vae.decoder(z, training=False)), nan=0.5), 0, 1)

Any generator of windows of the same shape (N, T, 3) in the same channels can replace the VAE (pool_suites, EXTENDING.md); every assembly method of a suite takes the same pool.

docs.title: Utility: TSTR versus TRTR
docs.text:
The quality of the synthetic data is tested as follows: a model is trained only on synthetic data (TSTR — train on synthetic, test on real) and compared with the same model trained on real train (TRTR — train on real, test on real). Both are tested on the same real data (val / OOT); synthetic data never get there. The closer TSTR is to TRTR, the better the synthetic data. Features and labels of the synthetic data are computed on the synthetic data themselves. Example: the binary "tail" task (change over h steps above a train quantile) and a point forecast.

import pandas as pd

LAGS = (1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 168)
h = 24
d = train[h:] - train[:-h]
thr = np.nanquantile(d, 0.90)                    # the threshold is fixed on train

def tail_up(values):                             # label at t: change over the next h steps above thr
    v = np.asarray(values, float)
    dd = np.full(len(v), np.nan)
    dd[:-h] = v[h:] - v[:-h]
    return np.where(np.isnan(dd), np.nan, (dd > thr).astype(float))

def make_xy(values, how, task):
    """Features — lags and differences of the series, calendar; target — at horizon h."""
    v = pd.Series(values)
    X = pd.DataFrame({"v": v, **{f"d{l}": v - v.shift(l) for l in LAGS},
                      "sin": np.sin(2 * np.pi * how / 168), "cos": np.cos(2 * np.pi * how / 168)})
    y = tail_up(values) if task == "clf" else v.shift(-h).to_numpy()            # class / value forecast
    ok = X.notna().all(axis=1).to_numpy() & ~np.isnan(y)
    return X[ok].to_numpy(), y[ok]

# real part
Xr, yr = make_xy(train, how[:n_train], task)
# synthetic part: a method's series of length K·T in the channels, back to real units
sv, show = from_channels(series, lo, hi)
Xs, ys = make_xy(sv, show, task)

variants = {"TRTR": (Xr, yr),                    # real train
            "TSTR": (Xs, ys)}                    # the method's synthetic data only

Model and metric:

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, mean_absolute_error

Xte, yte = make_xy(test_values, test_how, task)       # real val / OOT

for name, (X, y) in variants.items():
    if task == "clf":
        m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y)
        print(name, "AUC", roc_auc_score(yte, m.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]))
    else:
        m = Ridge().fit(X, y)
        print(name, "MAE", mean_absolute_error(yte, m.predict(Xte)))

How to compare. The benchmark uses 10 seeds (a seed sets the generator, the assembly and the model), the differences TSTR(method) − TRTR and TSTR(method) − TSTR(random path) on the same test rows, and intervals by a block bootstrap over time (block = one week). The null reference for an assembly effect is the difference between two independent random assemblies of the same pool (vae_rand versus vae_rand_b, mid and max); in min, without the twin, it is the difference of vae_rand between neighbouring seeds (the pool is resampled on every seed, so this reference is wider).

docs.title: What must not be broken
docs.text:
• The scaler, the task thresholds, any reference statistics a method takes from the real data, and generator training — on train only.
  • The generator sees only train core windows; holdout is used only for early stopping.
  • Synthetic features are computed on the synthetic series, without lags across the boundary with the real one.
  • N ≥ K; every method yields a synthetic series of the same length K·T.

docs.title: Published runs
docs.text:
Two runs of profile min are published. They use the same code, configuration, datasets, task thresholds and seeds and differ in hardware.

Main run Replication run GPU 1× NVIDIA H200 (143 GB), computing infrastructure of darya.ai 1× NVIDIA L4 (24 GB), Google Colab CPU cores 192 12 System Ubuntu 22.04.5, driver 580.173.02; Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.20.0 Google Colab (Linux 6.6); the pinned requirements of envs/ (exact versions not recorded) Methods 34 run, 24 ranked: the min suite on the VAE pool and on the zEDGE pool, the four open long-series generators and zEDGE_TS (zedge_ts_long, zedge_ts_ar) 18 run, 13 ranked: the min suite on the VAE pool and the four open long-series generators Role every result of the paper, the leaderboard shown everywhere, the cost reproduction check Folder artifacts/run_h200/ (tables and reports; unit files on Hugging Face, run_h200/) artifacts/run_l4/ (tables and reports; unit files on Hugging Face, run_l4/)

Ranks are computed within one run, and times measured on different hardware are not compared. The main run contains its own copy of the 13 ranked methods of the replication run; ranked among themselves, they are compared with the replication run:

  • Kendall's τ between the two orders is 0.64; the first method is the same;
  • every mean rank of the main run lies inside the 95 % interval of the replication run, and 12 of 13 mean ranks of the replication run lie inside the intervals of the main run;
  • the top tier is the same except for vae_greedy, at its boundary (outside on the L4, p = 0.05 after Holm; inside on the H200);
  • places 2 to 4 hold the same methods in a different order; the largest shifts are vae_zseries (4th → 2nd) and vae_rand (7th → 12th).

Sources of the differences, from the per-unit tables of the two runs:

  1. Trained generators — the main source. The VAE (TensorFlow) and Diffusion-TS are retrained on another GPU and software stack; early stopping chooses other epochs (VAE: up to 148 epochs apart), so the weights, the pools and every method built on them differ (median relative difference of F1.2 between the runs: 9–28 % for the methods of the VAE pool, 13 % for Diffusion-TS).
  2. Sampling. Chronos is not trained, but with the same seeds it samples other trajectories on another GPU (median relative difference of F1.2: 48 %).
  3. Downstream models. On identical series (the real series, TimesFM, Timestral) the utility scores coincide in the median; the largest difference is 0.03 in AUC and 0.04 in MASE.
  4. Data. The prepared ETT series of the main run (content hash 30545d98975f96a4) differs at the value level from that of the replication run (a84f966b14c63b36, the published hash in marathonts/bench/data_hashes.json), with the same length, split and dates. The cause is not established: the series that the source gives today (checked on 29 October 2026) is identical to the replication run's, so prepare does not warn, and a new run reproduces the ETT data of the replication run, not of the main run. The effect on the metrics is small (at most 3·10⁻⁴ for the real series); the other eight datasets are identical in both runs.

The deterministic TimesFM and Timestral produce the same series on both GPUs and the same fidelity values, which confirms the attribution. The reported uncertainty covers the variation between runs, and the leaderboard is read by tier, not by place (HYPOTHESES.md, "Uncertainty and tests"): tier membership reproduces up to a borderline method, the exact place within the tier does not.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
The benchmark is not tied to hardware: the torch part (assembly, Diffusion-TS, Chronos, models linear and mlp, heavy fidelity metrics) runs on CUDA if available, otherwise on CPU; the gbdt model (XGBoost; scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting on macOS or without xgboost, CPU only) runs on the device set in marathonts/bench/model_configs.json ("device": "cpu" in min and mid, "auto" — CUDA if available — in max); the VAE (TensorFlow) runs on GPU if TensorFlow sees it, otherwise on CPU. TensorFlow is switched to incremental GPU memory growth so that torch in the same process does not run out of memory. Assembly computes in float64, so Apple MPS is not used. TPU is not used. The recommended runtime is GPU.

Each timing record stores the hardware (gpu, cpu_count, platform) and library versions. To compare time, all methods of one dataset must be run on the same type of hardware. Hypothesis testing warns if the timing table contains more than one GPU type.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
Stages are sequential. Each unit of work writes its own files and is skipped if they already exist and were made with the same settings: the record of each unit (pool, trained replica, shared Diffusion-TS model, series, labels) holds a fingerprint unit_fp — a hash of the data settings (data_key, not the contents of the data), the settings of its components, the contents of target_params*.json / model_configs.json (where they matter) and the fingerprints of the units it is made from. Change, for example, knn_k (the setting of vae_knn), and its series and everything computed from them are redone, while the VAE pools and the other assemblies are kept. Processed data store a data-settings key (data_key: only split, number of points and T): prepare redoes them if these settings changed, and the other stages refuse to read them otherwise. Keys are per dataset: a setting of one dataset only (Config.DATASET_KEYS, the Bitcoin window bitcoin_start / bitcoin_end) enters that dataset's keys, and a unit depends on the task thresholds of its own dataset only; the other datasets hash those settings at fixed values (PINNED_KEYS) and the thresholds of the other built-in datasets enter at the values of the frozen copies marathonts/bench/target_params*.pinned.json (never edit them). A changed Bitcoin window or changed thresholds of one dataset therefore redo that dataset only.

Utility and fidelity units are fingerprinted per cell (marathonts/bench/cells.py): a utility unit per task × model and the decision-transfer grid, a fidelity unit per metric group. Each cell's fingerprint holds only what it depends on (the series, the labels, that model's configuration; that group's settings, parameters and, for F8 / F11, the thresholds and tasks), and the cells a unit has done are listed in a registry next to it (cells.json, seed<k>.cells.json), written last. An added model, task or metric group computes only its own cells and adds them to the unit's files; a changed model or group redoes only its own; a failed cell is not listed and is retried on the next run; a unit without a registry has no done cells. A model's supported task kinds come from the environment (gbdt handles ms only with XGBoost installed), so run every stage in the same environment. The contents of the data are checked separately (§1b). Window slicing for generator training (max_windows, holdout_frac) and pool size (pool_size, pool_mult) are not stored in the data — they are computed from the config (data.window_layout) and enter only the fingerprints of what depends on them. Pool generator training and pool sampling have different fingerprints, and generator weights are stored with the record: a changed pool size resamples the pools from the already trained models and redoes the methods on the pools, while VAE and Diffusion-TS training, the pretrained generators (Chronos, TimesFM, Timestral), labels, TRTR and the fidelity of the real series are reused. Changed window slicings retrain the VAE and Diffusion-TS, but not the pretrained generators. The thresholds of an added dataset enter only the fingerprints of its own units: adding a dataset redoes nothing on the others. An error in one unit is written to artifacts/errors.log and does not stop the run; a utility unit in which all trainings failed is retried on the next run.

              0 raw ──────► data/raw/<ds>/*.parquet        (CSV/TXT → Parquet; download if missing)
                 │
              1 prepare ──► data/processed/<profile>/<ds>.parquet, <ds>.meta.parquet
                 │
              2 pools ────► artifacts/pools, generators      (in the generator's environment)
                 │
              3 generate ─► artifacts/series, records, generators (long-series generators)
                 │
              4 fidelity ─► artifacts/fidelity
                 │
              5 utility ──► artifacts/labels, utility (metrics, predictions, model weights)
                 │
              6 collect ──► artifacts/tables
                 │
              7 hypotheses ► artifacts/reports (Markdown), overall, leaderboard, metric_values, hypotheses

docs.title: 0. raw — marathonts/bench/datasets.py
docs.text: Source CSV / TXT files are converted to Parquet losslessly (float64, all columns); the original is deleted only after the row counts are checked. If the files are missing, they are downloaded from the links in the dataset registry.

docs.title: 1. prepare — marathonts/bench/data.py
docs.text:
• A dataset from the registry yields an hourly series (DATASETS.md): hourly mean (Electricity, Household, Jena), log of the last price of the hour (Bitcoin), as is (the rest).
  • Gaps of up to 6 hours are interpolated, longer ones stay NaN (windows with NaN are dropped). Metro: the continuous part after the 2014–2015 gap is taken. Bike: a missing hour = 0 rentals.
  • The last max_points points are taken (min: 10,000; max: the whole series).
  • Time-based split (min: 50 / 25 / 25, max: 60 / 20 / 20), with an embargo of 168 between parts.
  • On train: lo, hi for min-max, T = 168, K = round(n_train / T), N = max(pool_size, 2K) (pool_size = 300), slicing stride s (max_windows = 5000), core / holdout boundary (last 10% of train, embargo 168).

Profile min: all datasets have n = 9664, train = 5000, val = OOT = 2332, K = 30, N = 300, s = 1. Profile max:

Dataset n n_train K N ett 17,084 10,452 62 300 electricity 34,729 21,039 125 300 household 34,253 20,753 124 300 pjm 145,056 87,235 519 1038 beijing_pm25 43,464 26,280 156 312 jena 69,793 42,077 250 500 metro 28,636 17,383 103 300 bike 17,208 10,526 63 300 bitcoin 85,104 51,264 305 610

docs.title: 1a. targets — exogenous target parameters
docs.text: Task thresholds (for example, "change over 24 h above X") are set in advance for each dataset in marathonts/bench/target_params.json (max — marathonts/bench/target_params_max.json) and are only read during a run. Missing values (a new dataset or a new task) are proposed by the task's rule on train when the prepare stage meets them, and written to the file; the targets stage does the same on its own. The file is then reviewed and committed. Without parameters the stages fail with a hint. The file remembers which split the thresholds were computed on (_split_key): with another split (other max_points, split, embargo) it is not read — otherwise thresholds could come from the val or OOT of a run.

docs.title: 1b. hashes — content of the published data
docs.text: The sources can change after a run: a Kaggle dataset is re-uploaded daily (Bitcoin) and may revise its history, a file may be replaced. Fingerprints do not see this (they hash the data settings, not the data), so marathonts/bench/data_hashes.json stores a content hash of each prepared series of the published results, per data-settings key: time, value, hour of week and split, independent of the Parquet writer. prepare and loading the prepared data compare against it and warn once per dataset if the series differ — the run goes on, but its results are not comparable with the published ones. Datasets without a published hash (custom ones, other data settings) are not checked. The hashes stage (not part of all) adds the missing hashes for the current settings and never overwrites existing ones; run it once after prepare of a run that will be published and commit the file. The file is not part of any fingerprint: adding hashes redoes nothing.

docs.title: 2. pools — marathonts/bench/methods.py, marathonts/bench/generators/
docs.text: For each (dataset, pool generator, seed) — a pool of N windows (N, T, 3) and its record (training and sampling time, diagnostics). VAE (Protocol: pool generator, above): tsgm vae_conv5 + BetaVAE, latent 16, β = 2, early stopping on holdout; trained once per dataset (min) or on every seed (mid, max), sampled on every seed. The pool is shared by all methods with this generator, so vae_* differ only in the choice, order and joining of windows. The stage runs in the generator's environment (envs/tsgm.txt); generate computes a missing pool itself when the generator's modules are importable there.

docs.title: 3. generate — marathonts/bench/methods.py, marathonts/bench/generators/, marathonts/bench/assemblers.py
docs.text:
For each (dataset, seed, method) of methods (the methods of frozen_methods are skipped) — a series of length K·T in real units, hour of week, the index of the pool window and of the chunk at each point, a seam flag.

  • Assembly: every assembler takes the shared pool and returns K windows in order (with seam processing — more, and the series is cut to K·T). Each alternative assembler uses the seam criterion of its own literature (BASELINES.md A); the solvers vae_greedy, vae_atsp, vae_pctsp get the jump at the seam — the Euclidean distance between the last point of a window and the first point of the next over every channel (seam_jump). vae_zseries is zseries, the proprietary assembler of zypl.ai (under development): its results are published (Config.frozen_methods), its code is not part of the repository; generate skips it and its seam-processing variants.
  • Diffusion-TS (profiles min and mid — once per dataset, weights in generators/<ds>/diffusion_ts/seedshared.parquet, training time recorded for every seed — and max — on every seed): model from the official repository (external/Diffusion-TS), hyperparameters Config/etth.yaml with window length T; training by the official recipe (engine/solver.py): 18 000 steps, batch 128 with gradient accumulation 2, Adam from 1e-5 with warm-up to 8e-4 over 500 steps, then ReduceLROnPlateau on the training loss, EMA of the weights (0.995 every 10 steps, as ema-pytorch 0.2.1). Deviations, the same for every generator of the benchmark: early stopping on the holdout windows, as for the VAE; imputation — fast_sample_infill with 50 DDIM steps (the repository's imputation config uses 200), for generation time. The calendar channels are known at all window positions (hour of week continues from a random start, different for each seed), the model completes only the value.
  • Chronos: amazon/chronos-t5-small (max: chronos-t5-base), no fine-tuning, the library's default sampling (temperature 1, top-k 50, top-p 1), context 512, bfloat16 on GPU (chronos-forecasting 2.3.2). The series is one sample path grown in chunks of 64 (the model's prediction length), each chunk conditioned on the previous ones — the same as the library's predict(prediction_length=K·T, num_samples=1), which feeds the median of the samples (here the only sample) back as context. Its training corpus (Ansari et al., 2024, Table 3) contains Electricity (UCI, 370 clients, 15 min / hourly / weekly) up to the last 24 points, so on electricity Chronos has seen the val and OOT periods: its results there are not out-of-sample (DATASETS.md). The corpus also holds KDD Cup 2018 (Beijing air quality, 2017–2018), related to beijing_pm25: Chronos is left out on electricity and beijing_pm25. ETT is used by Chronos for zero-shot evaluation only; the other datasets are not in the corpus. Loaded once per process; the loading time is recorded as fit_wall_s of each seed.
  • TimesFM and Timestral: pretrained point forecasters used strictly as documented, zero-shot, package defaults, no sampling. The context is the whole train split (within the model's limit: 15 360 and 32 768 steps); the series is the median forecast of the K·T steps after it — TimesFM 3.0 (google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch, package timesfm 3.0.2) in one non-autoregressive pass, Timestral-209M (mistralai/Timestral-209M, package timestral) block by block (1024 steps), each block's median fed back as context (seams at the block boundaries). Model revisions are pinned (timesfm_revision, timestral_revision). A median forecast has no noise and is the same on every seed, so the between-seed spread is zero: in RQ2 the margin of their comparisons is the spread of the compared method (HYPOTHESES.md §2); they take part in the rankings and every other question. TimesFM 3.0 is trained on GiftEvalPretrain (built on LOTSA without the GIFT-Eval test sets, and without the sets overlapping fev-bench), Wikimedia Pageviews (to Nov 2023), Google Trends (to 2022) and synthetic data (model card). Electricity, ETT and Jena weather are GIFT-Eval test sets, so not in it; but it holds the household dataset itself (sceaux, UCI #235, value-identical 2007–2010), Beijing Air Quality (UCI #501: PM2.5 of 12 Beijing stations, 2013–2017 — the same city, pollutant and hours as beijing_pm25) and the Monash Bitcoin set (daily price, to 2021): TimesFM is left out on household, beijing_pm25 and bitcoin (exact and related pairs, DATASETS.md). Timestral's training data are not disclosed (mostly synthetic, real sets unnamed): its leakage cannot be checked. Licences of the weights: TimesFM 3.0 — TimesFM Non-Commercial License v1.0; Timestral — Modified MIT.

docs.title: 4. fidelity — marathonts/bench/fidelity.py
docs.text:
83 metrics F1–F12 from METRICS.md for each series (245 values: against three references), in 12 registered groups (custom groups via register_fidelity_group). Each metric is computed against three real references: the primary one is val (Config.fidelity_ref, no suffix), plus Config.fidelity_extra_refs (default train and OOT, suffixes @train, @oot). Train shows how well a method reproduces what it was trained on (methods trained on train, and methods that take reference statistics from train, use this data during fitting), val shows generalisation, OOT shows generalisation under drift. Group F10 (distance to train) is computed once. The pseudo-method real is a piece of OOT, so it is not evaluated against OOT. Three references triple the stage time (the F6.1 GRU discriminator is trained per reference); fidelity_extra_refs=[] evaluates against val only. Each metric has an orientation (ORIENT). Pairwise distances (MMD, nearest neighbours, precision / recall) and the GRU discriminator are computed in torch on GPU.

The pseudo-method real is the real OOT; the variants <method>@len are the method's series cut to the OOT length (for comparison with the ceiling at equal length, RQ0).

Metric How it is computed (formulas: METRICS.md) F5.7, F6.2 |AUC − 0.5| (*_auc_dev): ideal is indistinguishability F6.8, F10.1 |log of ratio| (*_logratio): ideal 0 (ratio = 1) F9.2 density |log density| (F9.2_density_logdev): ideal 0 (density = 1) F6.2, F6.6, F9 window features — 16 in-house statistics F6.8, F10 Euclidean nearest-neighbour distance F6.4 unbiased MMD² estimate (no diagonals), RBF with median bandwidth F5.5–F5.6 PELT on 2-hour means of the first 40,000 points F7.5 KS of drawdown from the rolling weekly maximum F7.6 weekly trend slope in std of the real series

docs.title: 5. utility — marathonts/bench/utility.py, marathonts/bench/models.py
docs.text:
Utility assesses the quality of the synthetic data: TSTR versus TRTR. For each (dataset, method, seed) × 14 tasks (U2.1–U2.9) × models × splits (val, OOT) a model is trained only on the method's synthetic data and compared with the same model trained on real data. Default models are linear, mlp (PyTorch) and gbdt (XGBoost, with a scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting fallback); description, parameters and libraries are in MODELS.md.

Regime Training R — TRTR (train on real, test on real) real train (pseudo-method real, once per seed) S — TSTR (train on synthetic, test on real) the method's synthetic series only

The closer TSTR is to TRTR, the more information useful to the model the synthetic data contain (transfer ratio in the ranking and in questions RQ1, RQ4, RQ5).

Features and labels of the synthetic data are computed on the synthetic data themselves, the test only on real data (BENCHMARK.md, Protocol: utility). Target thresholds come from train. Metrics (registry utility_metrics): AUC, PR AUC, Brier, log-loss, ECE, F1, lift (binary); macro AUC, log-loss, macro F1 (multiclass); MAE, RMSE, MASE, sMAPE, error on extremes (regression); pinball, coverage, share of quantile crossings (quantiles); MASE over the whole horizon and the last step (multi-step). Training and prediction time of each model are recorded. Only with decision_transfer (profile max) on the case-study task (stitch_task): a grid of 11 model configurations (U6.1) and threshold transfer from synthetic to real (U6.4).

docs.title: 6. collect — marathonts/bench/run.py
docs.text:
Gathers the files into artifacts/<profile>/tables/ — the published result of the benchmark. The rows of the methods of frozen_methods are taken from their unit files, or from the existing tables when there are none, for the datasets, seeds and settings of their published results only (tables/frozen.json, written by python -m marathonts.bench.run freeze; the rest is left out with a warning); config.json stores the paths inside the project relative to it:

Table Row = timing.parquet (dataset, method, seed): time, memory, diagnostics, hardware fidelity.parquet (dataset, method, seed): all F metrics utility.parquet (dataset, method, seed, task, model, regime, split): U metrics, time pools.parquet (dataset, pool generator, seed): training and sampling time, diagnostics cross_seed.parquet (dataset, method, seed pair): F9.4 — diversity across seeds datasets.parquet dataset: n, K, N, period, gaps inventory.parquet each artifact file: path, kind, size hardware.parquet, config.json hardware and library versions of the environment collect runs in (the hardware of each run is in timing.parquet), run configuration

Stage 7 (python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run, HYPOTHESES.md §7) reads these tables and writes the Markdown reports to artifacts/<profile>/reports/ — REPORT.md, OVERALL.md, LEADERBOARD.md, METRIC_VALUES.md — and their Parquet tables to hypotheses/, overall/, leaderboard/ and metric_values/.

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text:
Everything is in artifacts/<profile>/ (path — Config.artifacts_dir), Parquet with zstd compression; floats are float32, except series values (float64).

│                          seed<k>.record.parquet    training and sampling time, diagnostics
├── generators/<ds>/<generator>/seed<k>.parquet      generator weights (VAE, Diffusion-TS, SDV, custom)

│   ├── metrics.parquet                              U metrics

│   └── models.parquet                               weights of each trained model
├── tables/                                          summary tables (collect)
├── reports/                                         Markdown reports of stage 7:
│   ├── REPORT.md                                    research questions RQ0–RQ9, confirmatory family, case study
│   ├── OVERALL.md                                   overall leaderboard and its robustness checks
│   ├── LEADERBOARD.md                               rankings of every method in every slice
│   └── METRIC_VALUES.md                             values of the core fidelity metrics and the primary utility
│                                                    metrics by reference, dataset, task, model and split

│                                                    sensitivity, field, lodo, weights

│                                                    rankings_summary.parquet and others
├── metric_values/                                   fidelity.parquet, utility.parquet: median and IQR over
│                                                    seeds of every metric per dataset and method

Weights are loaded back into models without training — marathonts/bench/load.py:

from marathonts.bench import load
gen = load.load_generator(cfg, "ett", "tsgm_vae", seed=0)
m = load.load_model(cfg, "ett", "vae_zseries", 0, task="clf_up_h24_q90", model="gbdt", regime="S")
series = load.load_series(cfg, "ett", "vae_zseries", 0)

Pools are always saved (the separate environments work through them). The rest is controlled by the flags Config.save_generator_weights, save_model_weights (utility predictions are always saved — they are needed by hypothesis testing); weights_dtype="float16" halves the size of weight files (normalisation statistics always stay float32). In min a utility unit holds about 2 MB of predictions and 0.9 MB of model weights (every dataset has the same length there); in max the volume grows with the length of the series and the full boosting configuration.

docs.title: Compute volume
docs.text:
Generation units: 9 datasets × 10 seeds × 12 methods = 1080 series (mid: 13 methods, 1170 series; max: 31 methods, 2790 series; the 4 published methods are not generated); VAE trainings — 9 (min) or 90 (mid, max), Diffusion-TS trainings — 9 (min, mid) or 90 (max). The most expensive parts:

  • Diffusion-TS, generation: the series is built autoregressively, T/2 new points per step; for PJM — about 1000 sequential imputations of 50 DDIM steps per seed.
  • Assemblers on long datasets (PJM: K = 519, N = 1038): vae_pctsp runs up to pctsp_solutions solutions (at most pctsp_time_s) per unit.
  • Utility: per unit (TSTR; TRTR — once per dataset and seed), 14 tasks × 2 models (linear, gbdt) plus the MLP on one task (clf_up_h24_q90) in min and mid (29 fits; 14 × 3 = 42 in max), each tested on 2 splits. Models on GPU (torch, XGBoost) are the main speed-up; on CPU one ETTh1 unit takes a few minutes. Units are independent: they can be distributed across sessions (--datasets, --seeds).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every setting of the benchmark is a field of one dataclass, Config (marathonts/bench/config.py). A run is defined by a Config object: the stages of python -m marathonts.bench.run, the notebooks and the analysis all read it. This file describes how the object is built, the four ways to change it, every field with its default, the exogenous files, and which stages a change recomputes. How to run the stages is in GETTING_STARTED.md, how to add components in EXTENDING.md.

docs.title: How the configuration works
docs.text:
• Config() is profile min. Config.profile("min" | "mid" | "max", **fields) returns a profile with some fields changed; Config.quick(**fields) returns the smoke-test configuration.
  • When the object is created (__post_init__), the plugin files of plugins are imported, the assembly suite is registered on every pool generator of pool_suites, the long-series generators of long_methods are registered as methods, and — if methods is None — the method list is built from these fields. Methods that are switched off (disabled), published without code (frozen_methods) or the noise twin without noise_twin=True are removed from methods and baselines.
  • Components are named by their registry names (marathonts/bench/registry.py); the parameters of a component go to extra[<component name>] and reach it as ctx.params (generators, assemblers, fidelity groups) or self.params (models).
  • Each profile has its own folders, data/processed/<profile>/ and artifacts/<profile>/, so results of different profiles do not mix (mid reads the processed data of min, which are identical).

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
The settings that differ between the profiles are compared in BENCHMARK.md, "Profiles". The fields each profile sets:

Every other field is the min default.

docs.title: (a) Command-line flags
docs.text:
python -m marathonts.bench.run <stage> [flags] (marathonts/bench/run.py):

Flag Meaning stage raw, prepare, targets, hashes, pools, generate, fidelity, utility, collect or all (= raw … collect, without targets and hashes) --profile {min,mid,max} the profile (default min) --quick Config.quick() instead of the profile --config FILE a JSON file written by Config.to_json(); replaces --profile and --quick (d) --datasets NAME … Config.datasets --methods NAME … Config.methods: run exactly these methods (minus disabled and frozen_methods) --models NAME … Config.models (utility) --seeds N … Config.seeds --pool-generators NAME … stage pools: which pool generators to fit (default: those used by methods) --artifacts-dir DIR Config.artifacts_dir --device DEV Config.device for torch: cpu, cuda, cuda:1, … (default: CUDA if available) --diffusion-ts-dir DIR Config.diffusion_ts_dir, the clone of the Diffusion-TS repository --plugins FILE … plugin files, imported before the configuration is built and added to Config.plugins

The scope flags are applied on top of the profile, --quick or --config; a flag given without values is ignored. Every other field is set by (b), (c) or (d). Examples:

python -m marathonts.bench.run all --profile mid --datasets ett jena --seeds 0 1 2
python -m marathonts.bench.run generate --methods vae_greedy vae_knn chronos --device cuda:1
python -m marathonts.bench.run utility --models linear gbdt sk_hgb
python -m marathonts.bench.run all --plugins my_plugins.py --config my_cfg.json

The flags of the analysis are listed in Command line of the analysis.

docs.title: (b) The cfg cell of the notebooks
docs.text:
The setup cell of every notebook creates cfg = Config.profile(PROFILE); notebooks 01–06 then change it in their scope cell. The cell as shipped, with the optional lines commented out:

# ── scope of this run: change freely; finished units are skipped on re-run ──
import dataclasses
cfg = dataclasses.replace(
    cfg,
    datasets=list(cfg.datasets),  # the profile's datasets (marathonts/bench/config.py DATASETS); or a list, e.g. ["ett", "my_ds"]
    methods=None,                # None → the suites on every pool + long_methods; or a list to run a subset
    baselines=None,              # None → long_methods (case study: CS9, CS10)
    # custom components (EXTENDING.md): plugin files + one line each, no code changes:
    # plugins=["my_plugins.py"],                          # files registering them (path from the project folder)
    # pool_suites={"vae": "tsgm_vae", "gan": "my_gan"},   # the whole suite on another pool generator → gan_zseries, …
    # extra_assemblers=["my_stitch"],                     # an assembler on every pool → vae_my_stitch, …
    # extra_joiners=["my_smooth"],                        # your own seam processing (run like the built-in ones)
    # smooth_paths=["zseries", "greedy"],                 # assemblers that get seam processing ("all": all but the random path and vae_quilting; min: ["zseries"])
    # joiners=["crossfade", "wsola"],                     # which seam processings (None: all)
    # disabled=["pctsp", "chronos"],                      # switch off methods or components by name
    # noise_twin=True,                                    # + the noise twin vae_rand_b (min: off; mid, max: on)
    # frozen_methods=[],                                  # published results kept as they are, not run (default: vae_zseries and its
    #                                                     #   seam-processing variants, marathonts/bench/config.py FROZEN_METHODS); [] → left out of the tables
    # long_methods=[*cfg.long_methods, "my_long"],          # + a long-series generator (method and baseline)
    seeds=list(range(10)),
)

Any other field is added to the same call, e.g. knn_k=10, hpo=True or extra={**cfg.extra, "my_stitch": {"alpha": 0.5}}. The cell must be the same in every notebook of a run. Notebook 02 hands the whole cfg to its stage subprocess (run_in_env(..., config=cfg)). Notebook 07 does not use the scope cell: the analysis takes the configuration saved with the tables (Analysis-only settings).

docs.title: (c) Python
docs.text:
import dataclasses
from marathonts.bench.config import Config
from marathonts.bench.run import STAGES

cfg = Config.profile("min", hpo=True, datasets=["ett", "jena"], seeds=[0, 1, 2])
cfg = dataclasses.replace(cfg, knn_k=10, extra={**cfg.extra, "mlp": {"epochs": 50}})

for stage in ("raw", "prepare", "pools", "generate", "fidelity", "utility", "collect"):
    STAGES[stage](cfg)                      # or: from marathonts.bench.run import stage_generate; stage_generate(cfg)

from marathonts.hypotheses.run import main
main(["--profile", "min", "--artifacts-dir", str(cfg.artifacts_dir)])

Two rules apply to the method list:

  • Config.profile(...) and Config.quick(...) rebuild methods when a field that defines it (pool_suites, extra_assemblers, extra_joiners, long_methods, smooth_paths, joiners, disabled, noise_twin, frozen_methods) is passed without methods, and rebuild baselines when long_methods is passed without baselines.
  • dataclasses.replace(cfg, ...) keeps the list of cfg: pass methods=None (and baselines=None) with such fields, as the notebook cell does. disabled and frozen_methods are applied in either case.

extra replaces the whole dictionary: extra={**cfg.extra, ...} keeps the parameters the profile sets (max sets mlp and gbdt).

docs.title: (d) A JSON file
docs.text:
Config.to_json() writes every field; Config.from_json(text) reads it back. --config hands such a file to python -m marathonts.bench.run and python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run (the notebooks use it for their stage subprocesses):

from marathonts.bench.config import Config
cfg = Config.profile("min", seeds=[0, 1, 2], knn_k=10, disabled=["pctsp"])
open("my_cfg.json", "w").write(cfg.to_json())

python -m marathonts.bench.run all --config my_cfg.json
python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run --config my_cfg.json

The paths in the file (*_dir, *_file) are absolute paths of the machine that wrote it. For another machine or a Docker container, write them relative to the project folder; relative paths are resolved against the working directory, i.e. the project folder (/app in the containers):

import json
from pathlib import Path
from marathonts.bench.config import ROOT, Config

d = json.loads(Config.profile("min", seeds=[0, 1, 2]).to_json())
d = {k: (Path(v).relative_to(ROOT).as_posix() if k.endswith(("_dir", "_file")) and v else v) for k, v in d.items()}
Path("artifacts/my_cfg.json").write_text(json.dumps(d, indent=2))

collect writes the configuration of a run in this form to artifacts/<profile>/tables/config.json.

docs.title: Switching methods on and off
docs.text:
Every method is selected by the configuration; nothing in the code has to change.

  • Off. disabled takes method names ("vae_pctsp"), suite suffixes ("greedy" — on every pool) or component names: an assembler ("atsp"), a seam processing ("wsola" — all its variants), a pool generator ("tsgm_vae" — the whole suite on it) or a long-series generator ("chronos"). A switched-off method is not run and does not enter the baselines; its rows already in the tables are dropped by the next collect.
  • On. Built-in methods are on unless disabled. A custom one is switched on by its line: extra_assemblers, extra_joiners, long_methods, pool_suites (EXTENDING.md).
  • Seam processing over any assembler. smooth_paths=["greedy", "atsp"] adds every seam processing of joiners over these assemblers (vae_greedy_xfade, vae_atsp_wsola, …); "all" — over every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting (it has its own cut).
  • Only some methods. methods=["vae_rand", "vae_greedy", "chronos"] (or --methods) runs exactly this list.
  • Results without code. frozen_methods lists methods that are not run but whose results stay: generate, fidelity and utility skip them, collect carries their rows into the tables (from their unit files or, if there are none, from the tables already in tables/), and they take part in the rankings, the questions and the case study. Their rows enter only where the run has the settings of the published results: the dataset and seed are in the run, and the fingerprints the run gives them — what their series depend on in the open part (pool, data, thresholds) and each utility cell and fidelity group — equal those in tables/frozen.json (python -m marathonts.bench.run freeze, written once with the results). A run with other data, seeds, tasks, models or settings leaves the rest out with a warning, so its tables never mix the published numbers with its own. The default (bench.config.FROZEN_METHODS) is vae_zseries (zseries, the proprietary assembler of zypl.ai (under development)) and its three seam-processing variants, published as results; their code is not part of the repository, so the assembler zseries is never run on any pool. frozen_methods=[] leaves them out of the tables.

These fields, case_method, noise_pair and baselines enter no unit fingerprint. The analysis takes them from the configuration saved with the tables (tables/config.json); --config or the flags of the analysis change them for one analysis run.

docs.title: Analysis-only settings
docs.text:
Config.ANALYSIS_KEYS: they are never part of a fingerprint, so changing them re-runs only stage 7. Unlike the other fields, the analysis does not take them from tables/config.json but from the code defaults of the run's profile, then applies the command-line flags; python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run --config FILE uses the values of the file instead. Notebook 07 passes its cfg this way, so analysis settings set in its cfg cell (dataclasses.replace(cfg, core_metrics=…)) apply to the analysis.

Field Default Flag Meaning leaked {"chronos": ["electricity", "beijing_pm25"], "timesfm": ["beijing_pm25", "household", "bitcoin"]} --leaked JSON method → datasets in its training corpus, left out of the analysis (DATASETS.md); '{}' → none rank_exclude None --rank-exclude [METHOD …] methods left out of the rankings; None → the seam-processing variants unless every assembler has them; [] (flag without names) → rank every method utility_fail_penalty True --no-fail-penalty a TSTR cell a method's series could not train enters as a model that learned nothing; False → left out exclude_datasets [] --exclude-datasets DATASET … datasets left out of the analysis; their units stay on disk exclude_metrics [] --exclude-metrics METRIC … a fidelity id ("F6.1_disc_score" — every reference), one reference ("F6.1_disc_score@val"), a group prefix ending in . ("F12.") or a utility metric ("ece"; not a primary one) core_metrics None — core fidelity metrics per criterion (core rankings, overall leaderboard, METRIC_VALUES.md); None → hypotheses.leaderboard.CORE_METRICS metric_criteria {} — fidelity group → criterion, merged over leaderboard.FID_CRITERIA task_criteria {} — task type → utility criterion, merged over leaderboard.UT_CRITERIA (classification / regression enter the four rankings) primary_metrics {} — task type → primary utility metric, merged over catalog.PRIMARY_METRIC metric_orient {} — utility metric → +1 (higher is better) / -1, merged over the built-in metrics; a utility metric without one is not analysed near_copy_ratio 2.0 — memorisation flag of the overall leaderboard: near-copy share ≥ this × that of the real OOT piece (reported, not ranked)

The fields without a flag reach the analysis through a JSON file built from the run's saved configuration (the paths are set to those of this checkout):

import dataclasses
from pathlib import Path
from marathonts.bench.config import Config

base = Config.profile("min")                                    # the profile of the run
run = Config.from_json(Path("artifacts/run_h200/tables/config.json").read_text())
paths = {f.name: getattr(base, f.name) for f in dataclasses.fields(Config) if f.name.endswith(("_dir", "_file"))}
cfg = dataclasses.replace(run, **paths, metric_orient={"precision_top10": 1}, near_copy_ratio=3.0)
Path("analysis_cfg.json").write_text(cfg.to_json())

python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run --config analysis_cfg.json

At start the analysis warns about roles and choices the tables cannot serve: the noise pair or the case-study method missing, core metrics or a task type's primary metric missing, utility columns without an orientation.

docs.title: Parameters of components: extra
docs.text: Field Default Meaning extra {} {<component name>: {parameter: value}}: parameters of pool and long-series generators, assemblers, joiners (read from cfg in join), models (over model_configs.json) and fidelity groups

docs.title: Exogenous files
docs.text:
Two JSON files hold values that are fixed before a run and only read during it. Their contents enter the fingerprints of the units that read them, so an edit redoes exactly those units.

marathonts/bench/model_configs.json (Config.model_configs_file) — hyperparameters of every ML model (MODELS.md): one object per model (linear, mlp, gbdt, sk_linear, sk_hgb, sk_mlp) and, under "grids", the candidate configurations of the search (hpo=True), each merged over the model's fixed values. A model receives model_configs_file[<model>] updated by extra[<model>]. A custom model gets its own object (or only extra). Editing one model's entry redoes that model's utility cells only.

{
  "gbdt": {"n_estimators": 100, "max_depth": 4, "learning_rate": 0.2, "max_bin": 64, "device": "cpu",
           "multi_strategy_ms": "multi_output_tree"},
  "grids": {"gbdt": [{"max_depth": 2}, {"max_depth": 4}, {"max_depth": 6}, {"max_depth": 8}]}
}

marathonts/bench/target_params.json (min, mid) and marathonts/bench/target_params_max.json (max) (Config.target_params_file) — task thresholds per dataset in real units, {dataset: {task: {parameter: value}}}, plus _split_key: the data settings each dataset's thresholds were computed on. prepare (and the stage targets) proposes the missing ones by the task's rule on the train split and writes them; review and commit the file. With other data settings (max_points, split, embargo) the file is refused for that dataset, because thresholds of another split could come from this run's val or OOT: point target_params_file to a new file, and prepare fills it from the new train split. Editing the thresholds of one dataset redoes its labels, its utility cells, the fidelity groups F8 and F11 and the assemblers that read thresholds (uses_targets) on that dataset only. The files marathonts/bench/target_params*.pinned.json are frozen copies used for this per-dataset fingerprinting and are never edited.

marathonts/bench/data_hashes.json holds content hashes of the published prepared data; it is written by the stage hashes and enters no fingerprint (BENCHMARK.md, stage 1b).

docs.title: What a change recomputes
docs.text:
Each unit stores a fingerprint of what it depends on (Config.unit_fingerprint, Config.COMPONENT_KEYS, marathonts/bench/cells.py); a stage redoes the units whose fingerprint changed and skips the others (BENCHMARK.md, "Stages"). Downstream units follow: a redone series redoes its fidelity and utility.

Change Redone datasets, seeds, methods, models, tasks, fidelity_groups extended only the added units or cells max_points, split, embargo, max_gap_interp, T prepare and every unit of every dataset (a new split also needs thresholds, see above) bitcoin_start, bitcoin_end the same, for bitcoin only max_windows, holdout_frac VAE and Diffusion-TS training and everything after them; not the pretrained generators vae_latent, vae_beta, vae_epochs, vae_patience, vae_min_epochs, vae_batch VAE training, the pools, the pool-based methods pool_size, pool_mult, vae_noise, pool_train_replicas the pools and the pool-based methods; a stored trained VAE is reused where it fits the new setting (pool_size, pool_mult, vae_noise resample from it) pctsp_*, mbb_*, knn_*, quilt_tol, herding_* that assembler's series join_overlap, join_wsola_shift the seam-processing variants (join_overlap also vae_quilting) dts_*, diffusion_train_replicas Diffusion-TS series; the shared model (min, mid) is retrained only when a training setting changes (dts_d_model … dts_ema_after, not dts_sampling_steps, dts_context_frac, dts_infill_*) chronos_*, timesfm_*, timestral_* that generator's series extra[<component>] the units of that component an entry of model_configs.json that model's utility cells thresholds of a dataset in target_params*.json that dataset's labels, utility cells, F8 / F11 and assemblers with uses_targets test_splits, hpo, hpo_val_frac, save_model_weights, weights_dtype every utility cell decision_transfer, grid_methods, model_grid_task the decision-transfer cell fidelity_ref, fidelity_extra_refs, disc_epochs, edge_overlap, stitch_task every fidelity group extra[<fidelity group>] that fidelity group disabled, frozen_methods, noise_twin, smooth_paths, joiners, pool_suites, extra_assemblers, extra_joiners, long_methods the method list: added methods are computed, removed ones are left out of the tables by the next collect statistics fields, case_method, noise_pair, baselines, analysis-only settings stage 7 only device, paths, save_generator_weights nothing

docs.text:
python -m marathonts.hypotheses.run (marathonts/hypotheses/run.py) — every report of stage 7:

Flag Meaning --profile {min,mid,max} profile (default min); the configuration saved with the tables takes precedence --artifacts-dir DIR the run to analyse (default artifacts/<profile>) --processed-dir DIR the prepared data (dataset descriptors of RQ7, CS15, CS12 subgroups) --out-dir DIR base folder of the results: DIR/reports/, DIR/hypotheses/, DIR/overall/, DIR/leaderboard/, DIR/metric_values/ (default: the artifacts folder) --only ID … only these questions / hypotheses (RQ2, CS3, …); no confirmatory family, overall leaderboard, ranking files or metric values --no-case-study only the research questions, the rankings and the metric values --plugins FILE … plugin files: hypotheses, tests, metrics --config FILE a JSON written by Config.to_json(), used instead of the saved configuration --case-method METHOD method of the case study (default Config.case_method) --noise-pair A B two random paths on the same pool --baselines METHOD … long-series baselines of the case study --case-task TASK task of the case-study cells CS7, CS10, CS12, CS13 (default Config.stitch_task) --rank-exclude [METHOD …] methods left out of the rankings; without names — rank every method --no-fail-penalty leave out the TSTR cells a series could not train --exclude-datasets DATASET … datasets left out of the analysis --exclude-metrics METRIC … metrics left out of the analysis --leaked JSON replaces Config.leaked ('{}' — nothing left out)

docs.title: Datasets for the experiments
docs.text: Open datasets on which the methods from BASELINES.md are compared by the metrics from METRICS.md. Licences are listed in DATASET_LICENSES.md.

docs.title: Principle: the same datasets for all tasks
docs.text:
All utility tasks (U2.1–U2.9) are built from a single target series of a dataset, so every dataset below is used in all 14 tasks (nine task groups U2.1–U2.9) — there is one set of datasets for the whole experiment. To this end, for all datasets:

  • a single target column is chosen (channel 0 of the pipeline);
  • the step is brought to one hour (aggregation by mean or sum), the calendar is the hour of week (BENCHMARK.md, Protocol: data);
  • the length after aggregation is ≥ 17,000 hours: with a 60 / 20 / 20 split (train / val / OOT, profile max, the full series) and T = 168 this gives K ≥ 60 windows, enough for h = 168 and for events with q = 0.99. Profiles min and mid take the last 10,000 hourly points of every dataset with a 50 / 25 / 25 split: 9,664 points after the embargoes, train 5,000, val = OOT = 2,332, K = 30 (artifacts/run_h200/tables/datasets.parquet).

docs.title: 1. ETTh1 — Electricity Transformer Temperature
docs.text:
Loads and oil temperature of a power transformer in China, July 2016 – June 2018, 1-hour step. Columns: date, six loads (HUFL, HULL, MUFL, MULL, LUFL, LULL) and the oil temperature OT. A standard long-horizon forecasting benchmark (Informer, Autoformer, etc.), with no missing values. The shortest in the set — the lower bound on length.

  • Source: github.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset, file ETT-small/ETTh1.csv
  • Paper: Zhou H. et al. Informer: Beyond efficient transformer for long sequence time-series forecasting. AAAI 2021

docs.title: 2. Electricity Load Diagrams 2011–2014
docs.text:
Electricity consumption of 370 clients in Portugal, 2011–2014, kW per 15 minutes. The first column is the time, the rest are clients; separator ;, decimal comma. Clients connected later have zeros at the start. The target series is the total load aggregated to hours: strong daily and weekly seasonality.

  • Source: UCI #321

  • Author: Trindade A., 2015

  • Leakage for Chronos: the Chronos training corpus contains this dataset (Electricity 15 min, hourly and weekly, all 370 clients, without only the last 24 points; Ansari et al., Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series, TMLR 2024, Table 3). The benchmark's target is the sum of the clients, so Chronos has seen the val and OOT periods of this series in aggregated form; its results on electricity are not out-of-sample.

docs.title: 3. Individual Household Electric Power Consumption
docs.text:
Consumption of a single household in France, December 2006 – November 2010, 1-minute step. Columns: Date, Time, active and reactive power, voltage, current, three sub-meters. About 1.25% of the rows are missing (marked ?). The target series is the hourly mean of Global_active_power. A noisy series with sharp peaks — a test on irregular dynamics.

  • Source: UCI #235
  • Authors: Hébrail G., Bérard A., 2012
  • Leakage for TimesFM: the TimesFM 3.0 training data (GiftEvalPretrain) include this dataset as sceaux (from BuildingsBench): one hourly series, 2007-01-01 – 2010-11-26, equal to the hourly mean of Global_active_power on every common hour after a 1-hour label shift. TimesFM is left out on household (Config.leaked).

docs.title: 4. PJM Hourly Energy Consumption (PJME)
docs.text:
Hourly consumption of the PJM East region (USA), 2002–2018, megawatts. The set also contains ~12 files for other PJM regions in the same format (Datetime, <REGION>_MW). The longest series in the set (largest K). There are isolated duplicates and gaps at the transitions to daylight saving time.

  • Source: kaggle.com/datasets/robikscube/hourly-energy-consumption
  • Primary data: PJM Interconnection LLC

docs.title: 5. Beijing PM2.5
docs.text:
PM2.5 concentration at the US Embassy in Beijing and airport weather, 2010–2014, 1-hour step. Columns: No, year, month, day, hour, pm2.5, DEWP, TEMP, PRES, cbwd, Iws, Is, Ir. pm2.5 has about 2000 missing values. A heavy right tail and smog episodes (tail tasks U2.1–U2.4).

  • Source: UCI #381
  • Paper: Liang X. et al. Assessing Beijing's PM2.5 pollution: severity, weather impact, APEC and winter heating. Proc. Royal Society A 471, 2015
  • Leakage for TimesFM: the TimesFM 3.0 training data (GiftEvalPretrain, built on LOTSA) include "Beijing Air Quality" (UCI #501: PM2.5 and weather of 12 Beijing stations, March 2013 – February 2017). It is another file, but the same city, pollutant and hours as this series over 2013–2014 — the period of the min window. TimesFM is left out on beijing_pm25 (Config.leaked).
  • Leakage for Chronos: the Chronos training corpus includes KDD Cup 2018 (air quality of Beijing and London stations, January 2017 – March 2018; Benchmark I of Ansari et al., 2024). Same city and pollutant, other stations and years: a related pair, so Chronos is left out on beijing_pm25 too.

docs.title: 6. Jena Climate 2009–2016
docs.text:
Weather station of the Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry (Jena), 2009–2016, 10-minute step, 14 variables: pressure, temperature, humidity, wind, etc. The target series is temperature averaged to hours. Strong daily and yearly seasonality with weak weekly seasonality — a check that the "hour of week" calendar does not impose spurious structure.

  • Source: Max Planck BGC Jena; ready-made file — jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip (Keras / TensorFlow)

docs.title: 7. Metro Interstate Traffic Volume
docs.text:
Hourly westbound traffic on I-94 (Minneapolis – St Paul), October 2012 – September 2018, plus weather and holidays. Columns: holiday, temp, rain_1h, snow_1h, clouds_all, weather_main, weather_description, date_time, traffic_volume. There are duplicate hours (several weather descriptions) and a large gap in 2014–2015. The duplicate hours are averaged, and the series starts after the last gap longer than 30 days (June 2015). Very strong weekly structure.

  • Source: UCI #492
  • Author: Hogue J., 2019

docs.title: 8. Bike Sharing (hourly)
docs.text:
Hourly number of Capital Bikeshare bicycle rentals (Washington, D.C.), 2011–2012, with weather and calendar. Columns of hour.csv: instant, dteday, season, yr, mnth, hr, holiday, weekday, workingday, weathersit, temp, atemp, hum, windspeed, casual, registered, cnt. Several hours are missing (zero demand) and are set to 0. Count data with a trend between years.

  • Source: UCI #275
  • Paper: Fanaee-T H., Gama J. Event labeling combining ensemble detectors and background knowledge. Progress in Artificial Intelligence 2, 2014

docs.title: 9. Bitcoin Historical Data
docs.text:
Minute-level OHLCV data for BTC/USD (Bitstamp), from 2012 to the present. Columns: Timestamp, Open, High, Low, Close, Volume. Before 2017 many minutes have no trades; the series is taken from bitcoin_start = 2017-01-01 to bitcoin_end = 2026-10-01 (exclusive). The target series is the log of the hourly close price. A financial series: weak seasonality, volatility clustering, heavy-tailed increments.

  • Source: kaggle.com/datasets/mczielinski/bitcoin-historical-data
  • Leakage for TimesFM: GiftEvalPretrain includes the Monash "Bitcoin" set (18 daily series, among them the Bitcoin price, 2009 – mid-2021). The same asset at a daily resolution: a related pair, so TimesFM is left out on bitcoin in every profile — also in min, whose window (2025–2026) lies after it (Config.leaked).

docs.title: Leakage into pretrained models
docs.text:
A dataset whose object is in a pretrained model's training data is not out-of-sample for it: the method is left out on that dataset in every ranking, question and case-study test (Config.leaked, bench.config.LEAKED); the other methods keep every dataset. The analysis always applies the list of the current code (not the copy saved with the tables), so a pair added later takes effect on the next run of notebook 7 without recomputing anything; --leaked replaces it from the command line.

Rule. Left out are both - exact pairs: the same data, the same source series, in the training corpus; - related pairs: the same object — the same dataset, the same city and pollutant, the same asset — at other stations, years or resolution, whether or not the periods overlap with the benchmark window.

Kept are pairs that share only the phenomenon (bike rentals in another city, gridded weather reanalysis) and datasets that a model uses only for evaluation.

The audit (October 2026) checked every model × dataset pair against the primary sources: Chronos — the paper's Appendix B, Table 3 (pretraining = pretraining-only sets + Benchmark I; Benchmark II is zero-shot evaluation only); TimesFM 3.0 — the model card and the full list of GiftEvalPretrain sub-datasets (Hugging Face Salesforce/GiftEvalPretrain, LOTSA builders of uni2ts), with the candidate sub-datasets downloaded and compared with the benchmark's raw files; Timestral — the model card and the release note.

• CC BY-ND 4.0 (ETTh1). The licence allows sharing the dataset unchanged, and producing adapted material, but not sharing adapted material (§2(a)(1)(B), §3(a)(2)). Adapted material is material derived from the dataset and modified "in a manner requiring permission under Copyright and Similar Rights". Whether numeric measurements, synthetic series sampled from a generator trained on them, or the generator weights are adapted material in this sense is not settled. This project takes the conservative reading and withholds them (next section).

docs.title: Primary sources
docs.text:
The licence is set by whoever published the dataset; the primary data may have their own terms. Checked against the sources in October 2026.

PJM's current data service, Data Miner 2, states that redistribution of information or data contained in or derived from Data Miner 2 requires a PJM-issued Redistribution License, and its terms limit non-members to internal business use. The benchmark does not distribute the PJM data (raw downloads them from Kaggle); whether these terms apply to artifacts derived from the Kaggle copy is a legal question for the publisher of the artifacts; this project does not distribute artifacts derived from PJM data ("What is published").
  • Bitcoin (#9): the Kaggle dataset acknowledges the Bitstamp API as its source.
