docs.title: Figure 4 — Data preprocessing
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig04_data_preprocessing.pdf

Suggested caption. From raw files to model inputs. Each dataset becomes one hourly univariate series. The series is split in time with embargoes. All statistics (scaler, window length, number of windows, task thresholds) are fitted on the training split only. The series is then encoded as three channels in [0, 1] and cut into windows (red box: the leakage boundary).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Sources. Nine public hourly-or-finer datasets: ETTh1, Electricity Load Diagrams, Household Power, PJM (PJME), Beijing PM2.5, Jena Climate, Metro Traffic, Bike Sharing, Bitcoin (DATASETS.md).
  2. raw. Lossless conversion to Parquet (float64, all columns). The original file is removed only after the row count matches.
  3. Hourly univariate series. Hourly mean (Electricity, Household, Jena), last log-price of the hour (Bitcoin), as is (others).
  4. Gaps. Gaps of up to 6 h are interpolated. Longer gaps stay NaN, and windows that contain NaN are dropped. Metro uses the continuous part after the 2014–2015 gap; a missing Bike hour means 0 rentals.
  5. Length. Last max_points points (profile min: 10 000; max: full series).
  6. Temporal split with a 168 h embargo between parts. Profile min: 50/25/25; max: 60/20/20.
  7. Fitted on train only. Min–max bounds lo, hi; window length T = 168; number of assembled windows K = round(n_train / T); pool size N = max(300, 2K); stride s chosen to give about 5 000 training windows; task thresholds (from the committed target_params*.json).
  8. Channels. Channel 0 is the scaled value. Channels 1–2 are (sin + 1)/2 and (cos + 1)/2 of the hour of week (period 168).
  9. Windows. (n, T, 3) with stride s. Train is divided into core (generator training) and holdout (last 10%, early stopping), separated by an embargo of 168 rows (Config.embargo).

docs.title: Where each output goes
docs.text: Core windows → generator training. Holdout windows → early stopping. Full train → reference statistics of the methods that use them. Val → primary fidelity reference and utility test. Train and OOT → the other fidelity references (@train, @oot). OOT → utility test.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• In profile min every dataset has n = 9 664, train = 5 000, val = OOT = 2 332, K = 30, N = 300.
  • data_key = hash(split, max_points, T) is stored with the processed data. The other stages refuse to read processed data whose key does not match the configuration.

docs.title: Figure 5 — Temporal split and the role of each part
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig05_temporal_split.pdf

Suggested caption. Temporal split (profile min, drawn to scale). Hatched bars are embargo gaps of 168 h, wide enough to cover every label horizon h ≤ 168 and the longest feature lag (168). Inside train, the last 10% is held out to stop generator training early. Every statistic the methods may use comes from train. Val is the primary fidelity reference; train and OOT are also references. Val and OOT are the utility test sets.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Top row: train (50%) | embargo | val (25%) | embargo | OOT (25%). In profile max the shares are 60/20/20 over the full series.
  • Bottom row: train broken down for the generators: core windows | embargo (168 rows) | holdout. Core and holdout windows do not overlap.
  • Labels above list what each part is used for.

docs.title: Design rationale (for the paper)
docs.text:
• Fidelity is measured against three real references: val (primary, no suffix), train (@train) and OOT (@oot). Train shows how well a method reproduces the data it was fitted on — methods fitted on train, and methods that take reference statistics from train, use this data during fitting; val measures generalisation and OOT generalisation under drift. Two of the four rankings measure fidelity against val and OOT (holdout_clf, holdout_reg), two against train (train_clf, train_reg).
  • Real-data ceiling. Pseudo-method real uses the OOT series as a "synthetic" series (RQ0). OOT is shorter than K·T, so each method is also scored on its first len(OOT) points (@len) to compare at equal length.
  • Utility uses the same real val and OOT rows for TSTR and TRTR. OOT checks robustness to a shift in time (RQ5).

docs.title: Figure 6 — Pool generator (β-VAE)
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig06_pool_generator_vae.pdf

Suggested caption. The window-pool generator. A convolutional β-VAE is trained on core training windows and stopped early on the holdout loss. After training, N windows are sampled from a shrunk prior and written to disk as the pool that every same-pool method shares.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: Item Value Architecture tsgm vae_conv5 encoder/decoder + BetaVAE, latent dimension 16 Loss reconstruction + β·KL, β = 2 Optimisation Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 64, up to 400 epochs Early stopping holdout loss after each epoch with z = μ; patience 50; best weights restored; epochs 1–150 are not eligible (vae_min_epochs), because holdout minima at early epochs give nearly flat pools Sampling z ~ 0.5 · N(0, I) → decoder → NaN replaced by 0.5 → clipped to [0, 1] Pool N = max(300, 2K) windows of shape (T, 3), per (dataset, seed)

docs.title: Model sharing across seeds (pool_train_replicas)
docs.text:
• min: one VAE per dataset (9 trainings in total); seeds change only the sampling.
  • mid, max: one VAE per seed (90).
  • Any other value k of pool_train_replicas gives k VAEs per dataset; seed s uses model s mod k.

The training time of a shared model is recorded for every seed and enters the cost comparison (RQ6) for each of them.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• The assembler does not depend on where the pool comes from. Any generator that outputs windows in the same three channels can replace the VAE (registry pool_generators; e.g. sdv_par, real_windows).
  • Fitting and sampling have separate fingerprints. Changing N re-samples the pools from the saved weights without retraining the VAE.

docs.title: Figure 8 — The compared methods
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig08_method_family.pdf

Suggested caption. The compared methods. Groups A and B take windows from the same VAE pool, so they differ only in which windows they pick, in what order, and how seams are handled. Group C generates long series directly. Every method returns one series of length K·T per (dataset, seed).

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A — Selection and order (10 methods in mid / max, 9 in min without vae_rand_b; same pool). vae_zseries (zseries, the proprietary assembler of zypl.ai (under development), the case-study method: its results are published (Config.frozen_methods), its code is not part of the repository); the control vae_rand (K random windows in random order) and, in mid and max, vae_rand_b (a second independent random order, used to estimate noise); alternative assemblers, each with the seam criterion of its own literature: vae_greedy (nearest neighbour by the jump at the seam), vae_atsp (asymmetric TSP over the whole pool with LKH via elkai; the cheapest run of K consecutive windows in the tour), vae_pctsp (prize-collecting TSP in OR-Tools: chooses K of N windows and their order at once; up to 2 000 solutions or 60 s) — the three solvers by the jump at the seam, the Euclidean distance between the last point of a window and the first point of the next (the frame distance of video textures); vae_mbb (matched-block bootstrap: a Gaussian kernel of the jump, bandwidth = median jump), vae_knn (k-nearest-neighbour resampling, k = √N, weights ∝ 1/rank), vae_quilting (image quilting: a random window among those whose overlap error is within 1.1 × the best, then the minimum-error cut), vae_herding (kernel herding towards train windows under MMD; random order).

B — Seam joiners (3 methods; 21 in max). Applied to the path of vae_zseries (published results; in max also to every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting). Neighbouring windows overlap by 12 points: xfade blends the overlap with a Hann window, wsola first shifts the next window by up to 12 points to the best correlation, and quilt cuts at the point of minimum difference (1-D image quilting). Overlap shortens the series, so the joiner takes more windows than K and truncates the result to K·T.

C — Long-series generators (4 methods). diffusion_ts (Diffusion-TS trained on the same training windows; series grown by autoregressive infilling), chronos (pretrained Chronos-T5-small, zero-shot, sampled), timesfm (TimesFM 3.0) and timestral (Timestral 209M): pretrained forecasters used zero-shot as documented — the median forecast of the K·T steps after train, the whole train as context (up to the model's limit), the same series on every seed. See Fig. 9.

Reference. real is not a method: in fidelity it is the OOT series (ceiling); in utility it is the model trained on real train (TRTR).

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• Scale: 16 methods in min (without vae_rand_b), 17 in mid, 35 in max, of them 4 published results (vae_zseries and its three joiner variants); the pipeline runs 12 / 13 / 31 methods × 10 seeds × 9 datasets = 1 080 / 1 170 / 2 790 generated series.
  • Every series is stored with its hour of week, the source window and piece of each point, and a seam flag. The seam metrics (F5) use the flag; for group C, chunk boundaries count as seams.
  • Source: marathonts/bench/methods.py, marathonts/bench/assemblers.py, marathonts/bench/joiners.py, BASELINES.md.

docs.title: Figure 9 — Long-series generators (Diffusion-TS, Chronos, TimesFM, Timestral)
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig09_long_generators.pdf

Suggested caption. The baselines that generate long series directly. Diffusion-TS grows the series by autoregressive infilling: each new window takes the last T/2 generated values as known context and fills in the rest. Chronos samples continuations of the end of the training series in chunks of 64 points. TimesFM and Timestral give their median forecast of the K·T steps after train, with the whole train as context (up to the model's limit). Boundaries between chunks or blocks count as seams in the seam metrics.

docs.title: Diffusion-TS
docs.text:
• Official implementation (external/Diffusion-TS, pinned commit), hyperparameters from Config/etth.yaml with window length T.
  • Trained on the same core windows as the VAE, with an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights; optimiser, learning-rate schedule (warm-up to 8e-4, then plateau decay), batch 128 with gradient accumulation 2 and EMA as in the official solver; early stopping on the holdout windows.
  • min/mid: one model per dataset; max: one model per seed.
  • Generation: the calendar channels are known at every position (hour of week continues from a random start, one per seed); only the value channel is generated. Window 1 is generated with no known values. Each later window takes the last c = T/2 values as known context and infills the remaining T/2 (fast_sample_infill, 50 DDIM steps). The result is truncated to K·T.

docs.title: Chronos
docs.text:
• amazon/chronos-t5-small (max: chronos-t5-base), no fine-tuning. Loaded once per process; the load time is recorded as fit_wall_s.
  • Context: the last 512 real training values. The model samples one path 64 points at a time; each chunk is appended and the context is cut back to the last 512 points.
  • The hour of week continues from the end of train.

docs.title: TimesFM 3.0 and Timestral 209M
docs.text:
• Pretrained forecasters used zero-shot as documented, package defaults, revisions pinned: google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch (package timesfm 3.0.2) and mistralai/Timestral-209M (package timestral).
  • Context: the whole training split (within 15 360 and 32 768 steps). The series is the median forecast of the K·T steps after train: TimesFM in one non-autoregressive pass (no seams), Timestral in blocks of 1024 steps with each block's median fed back (block boundaries are seams).
  • No sampling: the series is the same on every seed, so its between-seed spread is zero.
  • Leakage: Chronos is left out on electricity and beijing_pm25, TimesFM on household, beijing_pm25 and bitcoin (the same data or object in their training data, DATASETS.md); Timestral's training data are not disclosed (DATASETS.md).

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• Calendar handling differs across families. The VAE generates the calendar channels as part of the window, Diffusion-TS has them imposed, and Chronos, TimesFM and Timestral continue the real calendar. For this reason the calendar-continuity metrics F4.4–F4.5 are left out of the ranking and the cross-family comparisons (RQ1–RQ3, CS9).
  • Cost: for the longest dataset (PJM, profile max), Diffusion-TS needs about 1 000 sequential infills of 50 DDIM steps per seed.

docs.title: Figure 10 — Utility pipeline (TSTR vs TRTR)
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig10_utility_pipeline.pdf

Suggested caption. Utility protocol. Features and labels are computed separately on each series: real train, the synthetic series, and the real test parts. Thresholds are frozen on real train. Each model is trained either on real train (TRTR) or on the synthetic series only (TSTR) and evaluated on the same real val and OOT rows. Synthetic data never enters a test set.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Inputs. Real train; the synthetic series of method m (K·T points, real units); real val and OOT.
  2. Task parameters. Quantile thresholds per (dataset, task), fixed on real train and read from target_params.json.
  3. make_xy on each series separately (no lags across the boundary between series): 11 features (value; differences at lags 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 168; sin/cos of hour of week) and labels for 14 tasks (Fig. 11).
  4. Training regimes. R = TRTR (pseudo-method real, once per seed) and S = TSTR (every method, every seed). Models: linear, mlp (PyTorch) and gbdt (XGBoost), with fixed configurations from marathonts/bench/model_configs.json. Each model standardises features on its own training set.
  5. Prediction on the same real test rows (val and OOT).
  6. Prior correction (classification only). Classifiers are trained with balanced class weights. Their probabilities are mapped back to the class shares of their own training set, P(c|x) ∝ P_bal(c|x) · share_train(c), so Brier, log-loss and ECE measure calibration. AUC, PR AUC, lift and F1 are unchanged.
  7. Metrics (registry utility_metrics): binary: AUC, PR AUC, Brier, log-loss, ECE, F1, lift; multiclass: macro AUC, log-loss, macro F1; regression: MAE, RMSE, MASE (seasonal naive scale, lag 168), sMAPE, error on extremes; quantile: pinball, coverage, crossing rate; multistep: MASE over the horizon and at the last step.
  8. Outputs. Metrics, every prediction and the weights of every model, per (dataset, method, seed). The statistics compare TSTR(m) with TRTR (transfer ratio, RQ1, RQ4, RQ5) and with TSTR of other methods (RQ1–RQ3, RQ8–RQ9). Row-level block bootstrap tests use the saved predictions.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• The benchmark measures the quality of synthetic data, not its value as augmentation. Real + synthetic regimes are not included.
  • Optional, profile max only: hyperparameter search on the last 20% of real train (gap h + 168 rows), and the RQ5 (c) grid (11 model configurations, ranking agreement and threshold transfer).

docs.text:

File: fig11_tasks_models.pdf

Suggested caption. The 14 downstream tasks (U2.1–U2.9) and the models trained on each. All tasks use the same 11 features. Labels are functions of the series, with thresholds frozen on real train. Task U2.1 (green) is the task of the pre-specified case-study cell.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text: ID Task(s) Kind Target U2.1 clf_up_h24_q90 binary change over 24 h above the 0.90 train quantile U2.2 clf_up_h{1,6,168}_q90 binary same, other horizons U2.3 clf_up_h24_q{95,99} binary rare events U2.4 clf_down_h24_q10 binary change below the 0.10 quantile (opposite tail) U2.5 mc3_h24 3 classes down / neutral / up U2.6 reg_h{1,24,168} regression value x_{t+h} U2.7 qreg_h24 quantile regression quantiles 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9 U2.8 ms_h24 multistep vector x_{t+1..t+24} U2.9 vol_h24 volatility std of the next 24 hourly changes

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
• linear: logistic/softmax regression (L-BFGS, balanced weights, C = 1), ridge (α = 1, exact solve), linear quantile regression (smoothed pinball). PyTorch.
  • mlp: 64 → 32 ReLU network, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 512. In min/mid it runs 30 epochs on U2.1 only; in max, up to 200 epochs with early stopping on all tasks.
  • gbdt: XGBoost. min/mid: 100 trees, depth 4, 64 bins, CPU, vector leaves for the multistep task. max: 200 trees, depth 6, 256 bins, one ensemble per step.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• Every (task, model) pair is fitted in both regimes (S and R) and evaluated on both val and OOT.
  • Every task enters the ranking and the research questions with equal weight, grouped into classification and regression; U2.1 only marks the case-study cell (CS7), U2.2–U2.9 are case study CS8.
  • Source: marathonts/bench/tasks.py, marathonts/bench/models.py, MODELS.md, METRICS.md (U2–U4).

docs.title: Figure 12 — Fidelity evaluation
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig12_fidelity_evaluation.pdf

Suggested caption. Fidelity evaluation. Every generated series, the real OOT series (ceiling), and length-matched truncations of the generated series are scored by the same code against three real references: val (primary), train and OOT. The metrics are organised in 12 groups (83 metrics); memorisation (F10) is computed once, against train.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• Series under test: each (method, seed) series of length K·T; m@len, the first len(OOT) points of each method (seed 0), for an equal-length comparison with the ceiling; real, the OOT series (seed 0).
  • References: val (primary, no suffix); train (@train): how well a method reproduces the data it was fitted on — methods fitted on train, and methods that take reference statistics from train, use this data during fitting; OOT (@oot): generalisation under temporal drift. real is a piece of OOT and is not scored against OOT.

docs.title: Metric groups
docs.text: F1 marginal distribution · F2 increments · F3 temporal dependence (incl. ACF beyond the window length, T…3T) · F4 seasonality and calendar · F5 seams · F6 window-level distribution (post-hoc GRU discriminator, C2ST, predictive score, MMD, feature-FID, nearest-neighbour distance) · F7 long-range structure (rolling statistics, level crossings, drawdowns, trend, HMM regimes) · F8 target structure · F9 diversity and coverage · F10 memorisation · F11 class balance over every classification task (relative error of class shares, rare events, multiclass TVD, lost minority class) · F12 extremes and outliers (exceedances of the real 0.5 / 99.5% quantiles, local spikes, weekly block maxima and minima).

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• Each metric has an orientation (ORIENT, higher or lower is better).
  • AUC-type scores are reported as |AUC − 0.5|, ratios as |log ratio|; window features are 16 in-house statistics; nearest-neighbour distances are Euclidean.
  • Pairwise distances (MMD, nearest neighbours, precision/recall) and the GRU discriminator run in torch on the GPU. Cross-seed diversity (F9.4) is computed separately at the collect stage.
  • Source: marathonts/bench/fidelity.py, METRICS.md.

docs.title: Figure 13 — Statistical analysis pipeline
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig13_statistical_pipeline.pdf

Suggested caption. From benchmark tables to conclusions. The long-format tables feed three analyses applied to every method: a ranking of every method in every slice, paired comparisons A vs B measured in units of an empirical noise level, and associations across methods. A pre-specified confirmatory family (C1–C4) is corrected jointly; a case study of one method is reported separately as secondary.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Long format. One row per (dataset, seed, unit, method, value). A fidelity unit is a metric against one real reference (train, val, OOT); a utility unit is task × model × regime × split × metric (regime S = TSTR, R = TRTR).
  2. Ranking (RQ1). Methods are ranked within every leaf per (dataset, seed); ranks are averaged leaf → group → criterion × slice → domain → ranking with equal weights per level. Four rankings, each the mean of a fidelity domain (six criteria, without privacy) and a utility domain: fidelity against val + OOT or against train × utility classification or regression (TSTR on val and OOT). Privacy (F10) and cost are ranked separately; next to each ranking — the same ranking with cost as a third domain and the Pareto front "rank × time"; each domain is also ranked on its own; thematic slices (class balance, extremes) are reported alongside. Uncertainty: two-level bootstrap of ranks (CI, probability of first place and top 3); Friedman test; every method against the best by one-sided Wilcoxon with Holm (top tier); Kendall τ between slices; random criterion weights; the two random paths of one pool must be indistinguishable (mid, max).
  3. Noise = smallest effect of interest per dataset and unit: on one pool, the median |vae_rand − vae_rand_b| over seeds (in min, without vae_rand_b, the median |vae_rand(seed k) − vae_rand(seed k+1)|); for an independently trained method A, the median |A(seed k) − A(seed k+1)|.
  4. Paired comparisons (RQ0a, RQ2, RQ3, RQ5a, RQ8b, RQ9b): d = orientation · (A − B) on matching seeds, d > 0 ⇔ A better. B is a method, the median of all assembly methods of the pool, or a contrast (main effect of window selection, of seam processing).
  5. Per dataset (10 seeds): two one-sided Wilcoxon tests (α/2 each), TOST against ± noise, Hodges–Lehmann effect. Globally (9 datasets): effects in noise units, averaged over seeds; Wilcoxon, sign test, t-test, TOST ±1 noise unit, two-level bootstrap CI. Benjamini–Hochberg within a question.
  6. Verdict: better · worse · same (proven equivalence) · inconclusive.
  7. Associations (RQ0c–d, RQ4, RQ7, RQ8c, RQ9c): Friedman per metric (does it discriminate the methods beyond noise); Spearman ρ across methods within a dataset — metric ↔ metric, fidelity ↔ utility, dataset descriptor ↔ effect — then the median ρ and Wilcoxon over datasets, BH.
  8. Confirmatory family C1–C4: cells U2.1 (AUC) and U2.6 h = 24 (MASE), TSTR, linear model, OOT. C1 methods differ (Friedman); C2 Diffusion-TS and Chronos against the assembly median; C3 main effect of window selection; C4 main effect of seam processing. Joint Holm over the ten tests.
  9. Case study CS1–CS15 (secondary): one method (--case-method) against its controls on the same pool, the alternative assemblies and the long-series generators; row-level tests average predictions over seeds and compare ΔAUC on identical test rows by a block bootstrap over weeks (test rows are autocorrelated, so per-seed DeLong tests would be anti-conservative).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Reports in reports/: OVERALL.md, LEADERBOARD.md, METRIC_VALUES.md (values of the core fidelity metrics and the primary utility metrics by reference, dataset, task, model and split), REPORT.md. Tables: overall/, leaderboard/, metric_values/, hypotheses/RQ*_*.parquet, CS*_*.parquet, confirmatory.parquet. Source: HYPOTHESES.md, marathonts/hypotheses/overall.py, marathonts/hypotheses/leaderboard.py, marathonts/hypotheses/metric_values.py, marathonts/hypotheses/questions.py, marathonts/hypotheses/engine.py, marathonts/hypotheses/stats.py.

docs.title: Figure 14 — Research questions, evidence and analyses
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig14_hypotheses_map.pdf

Suggested caption. The research questions of the benchmark. RQ0 validates the benchmark itself, RQ1 ranks every method in every slice, RQ2–RQ9 compare families of methods and properties of the synthetic data. C1–C4 (red) form the pre-specified confirmatory family. The case study of one method is secondary.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Evidence colour: green = utility in TSTR/TRTR (Figs. 10–11), grey = cost records or dataset descriptors, white = fidelity (Fig. 12) and utility together.
  • Compared with: "rand" is the random path of the VAE pool; the "assembly median" is the median, per seed, of every assembly method of the pool; "seam-processing contrasts" are the main effects of each seam processing; A, B, C are the groups of Fig. 8.
  • Note: confirm. = confirmatory, explor. = exploratory, max only = needs the decision grid (profile max).

docs.title: Logic of the question set
docs.text:
• RQ0 checks that the benchmark can tell methods apart: two random paths of the same pool must not differ, real data (the ceiling) is compared with the synthetic series on every metric, and only metrics that separate the methods beyond noise should carry conclusions.
  • RQ1 is the leaderboard: four rankings (fidelity against val + OOT or against train × utility classification or regression on val and OOT); privacy, cost (time, memory) and the thematic slices for class balance and extremes are ranked separately.
  • RQ2 compares generating a long series whole with assembling it from short windows; RQ3 decomposes assembly into window selection and seam processing.
  • RQ4 asks which fidelity metrics, against which reference, predict utility. RQ5 measures the gap to real data and the stability of the ranking. RQ6 covers speed and cost. RQ7 looks for dataset properties associated with differences between families. RQ8 and RQ9 follow two properties that aggregate metrics do not isolate: class shares (rare events above all) and extremes.
  • Source: HYPOTHESES.md, marathonts/hypotheses/questions.py, marathonts/hypotheses/leaderboard.py.

docs.title: Figure 15 — Incremental recomputation with unit fingerprints
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig15_incremental_recompute.pdf

Suggested caption. Dependency graph of unit fingerprints. Each unit of work stores a hash of its inputs, its own settings, the relevant configuration files, and the fingerprints of the units it depends on. When a setting changes, only the units downstream of it are recomputed.

docs.title: What the figure shows
docs.text:
• Roots: processed data (data_key: split, number of points, T), the generator training windows (max_windows, holdout_frac), and two committed JSON files (target_params*.json, model_configs.json).
  • Generator training and sampling are separate units. VAE fitting depends on the training windows; pool sampling depends on the fitted weights and the pool size. Diffusion-TS fitting depends on the training windows; the loads of the pretrained generators (Chronos, TimesFM, Timestral) depend only on the data.
  • Series of a method depend on their upstream generator units and on the settings of their assembler or joiner (e.g. mbb_bandwidth, pctsp_*, join_overlap).
  • Evaluation units: fidelity depends on the series and the target parameters (of its own dataset: the thresholds of a new dataset do not redo the others); labels depend on the data and the target parameters; utility (TSTR) depends on the series, the labels and the model configurations; TRTR depends on the labels and the model configurations only. Fidelity and utility units are fingerprinted per cell (metric group; task × model): the done cells are listed in a registry next to the unit (cells.json), so an added or changed model, task or metric group computes only its own cells.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Changing knn_k (the number of neighbours of vae_knn) recomputes the vae_knn series (and its joiner variants, where they are run) together with their fidelity and utility. Pools, VAE weights, the other methods, labels, TRTR and the fidelity of the real series are kept. Changing the pool size re-samples pools from the stored weights and redoes every same-pool method, while VAE training, Diffusion-TS, the pretrained generators, labels, TRTR and real-data fidelity are kept.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• This makes long runs resumable across sessions (e.g. Colab disconnections) and keeps all cached results consistent with the current configuration.
  • A utility unit in which every fit failed (e.g. out of GPU memory) is not marked done and is retried on the next run.
  • Source: marathonts/bench/config.py (unit_fingerprint), BENCHMARK.md "Stages".

Suggested caption. Layout of the benchmark outputs. Every unit of work writes its own Parquet file. The collect stage merges them into the published tables in tables/.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• Storage: Parquet with zstd; float32 everywhere except series values (float64). Each profile writes to its own artifacts/<profile>/.
  • Every model and generator can be reloaded and used without retraining (marathonts/bench/load.py), so reviewers can re-evaluate saved models on new test data.

docs.title: Figure 17 — Run profiles
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig17_profiles.pdf

Suggested caption. The three run profiles. min (default, intended for Colab) shares one trained generator per dataset across seeds. mid retrains the VAE on every seed and adds the noise twin vae_rand_b. max uses the full series, retrains generators on every seed, and turns on hyperparameter search and the decision-transfer grid.

docs.title: Notes for the text
docs.text:
• What a seed varies depends on the profile. In max, VAE and Diffusion-TS are retrained on every seed, so per-dataset conclusions generalise over the training procedure. In min, seeds vary only pool sampling, random paths and model fitting, so conclusions are conditional on the trained generator. mid sits in between: the VAE is retrained on every seed, Diffusion-TS once per dataset.
  • min compares 16 methods, mid 17 (+ the noise twin vae_rand_b), max 35: in max every seam processing also runs over every assembler except the random path and vae_quilting, not only vae_zseries (smooth_paths="all"). Each count includes the 4 published results of frozen_methods (vae_zseries and its seam-processing variants), which the pipeline does not run. Without vae_rand_b (min) the noise is the between-seed spread of vae_rand. All profiles use the same 9 datasets and 10 seeds.
  • Profiles write to separate data and artifact folders, so their results never mix. Task thresholds come from target_params.json (min, mid) or target_params_max.json (max), because the min train split falls inside val/OOT of max.
  • Source: marathonts/bench/config.py (Config.profile), BENCHMARK.md.

docs.title: Figure 18 — Extension points
docs.text:
Vector PDF

File: fig18_extensibility.pdf

Suggested caption. Extension points. Every part of the benchmark is registered by name. A plugin file registers new components, and the configuration selects them. A new pool generator, assembler, seam joiner or long-series generator becomes part of the comparison and of the relevant hypotheses without changes to the benchmark code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A plugin (my_plugins.py) uses @registry.<kind>.register("name"), or the helpers register_task, register_method, register_fidelity_group, register_test, register_hypothesis.
  • Config loads the plugin everywhere: in every notebook, in subprocesses of other environments, and in the hypothesis part (the run configuration is stored in tables/config.json).
  • Automatic expansion: pool_suites adds the whole assembly suite on a new pool generator (<prefix>_zseries, <prefix>_rand, …); extra_assemblers adds an assembler on every pool, extra_joiners a seam processing over the assemblers of smooth_paths; long_methods adds a long-series generator as a method and a baseline; disabled switches off any method or component by name. New methods enter the ranking and the research questions automatically (their family is read from the method spec); the confirmatory family covers Diffusion-TS and Chronos.
  • Any method can be the subject of the case study (hypotheses.run --case-method … --noise-pair …).
  • Source: marathonts/bench/registry.py, EXTENDING.md.
